passages.happening:
“Command the Israelites to bring you pure oil of pressed olives for the light, to keep the lamps burning continually” (verse 2). Aaron is to tend the lamps on the gold lampstand ‘from evening until morning’ (verse 3).

Twelve loaves of fine flour are to be baked and set in two rows on the gold table before the LORD, with frankincense beside them (verses 5-7). “Every Sabbath day the bread is to be set out before the LORD on behalf of the Israelites as a permanent covenant” (verse 8). The priests eat the old loaves in a holy place (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
After the yearly feasts come two things that never stop: a light and a table.

Olive oil was the lamp fuel of the ancient world. Every house had its small clay lamps. The sanctuary received the finest oil, from olives beaten or pressed by hand. And it came from the people. They supplied the light of God's house.

The lamps burned through the night. The bread lay always on the table. Together they pictured a house where the host is at home. Whoever passed the tent in the dark knew that God had not gone away.

The twelve loaves stood for the twelve tribes of Israel. The whole people was set before God all the time, week after week, ‘as a permanent covenant’. Every Sabbath fresh loaves were laid out, and the priests ate the old ones.

One Hebrew word ties the passage together: continually. It is used of the lamps and of the bread. God's presence with Israel, and Israel's place before him, were to have no gaps.
passages.later:
The instructions were first given in Exodus: “And place the Bread of the Presence on the table before Me at all times” (Exodus 25:30).

When David was running for his life, a priest gave him this bread for his hungry men. Jesus recalled it: David “ate the consecrated bread, which was not lawful for them to eat, but only for the priests” (Matthew 12:4).

Jesus called himself “the light of the world” (John 8:12) and “the bread of life” (John 6:35). Readers have linked those sayings with the lamp and the bread of this chapter, though they are rooted more directly in other feasts and in the manna.
passages.asks: The people brought the oil that kept the light burning. Ask what you bring that keeps worship alive where you are. And ask what in your life with God is done ‘continually’, and what has gone out for want of tending.

passages.t: A man who cursed the Name
passages.happening:
“Now the son of an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father went out among the Israelites, and a fight broke out in the camp between him and an Israelite” (verse 10). “The son of the Israelite woman blasphemed the Name with a curse. So they brought him to Moses” (verse 11).

“They placed him in custody until the will of the LORD should be made clear to them” (verse 12).

The LORD answers. The man is to be taken outside the camp. Those who heard him are to lay their hands on his head, and the whole assembly is to stone him (verse 14). The rule is given for all time: “Whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD must surely be put to death”, and it holds “whether he is a foreign resident or native” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
This is one of only two stories in Leviticus. Like the first, the deaths of Nadab and Abihu, it is about a holy thing handled with contempt.

In that world a name was more than a label. It stood for a person's character and presence. To curse the name of God was to attack God himself. And in Israel God was king, and his presence in the camp was the people's life. So the act was a kind of treason against the covenant the whole community lived by.

The man had an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father. The story quietly raises a question. Did Israel's law apply to someone of mixed family? The answer is that there is one law for all. He is not judged more harshly for his father, and he is not excused.

Notice that no one acts in anger. The man is held until God's will is known. Only those who heard him give witness. The laying on of hands most likely declared that the guilt of the words lay on him and not on the hearers.

Later Jewish teaching took the offense to mean actually speaking God's personal name in a curse. This passage strengthened the Jewish custom of not saying that name aloud at all. Jews often speak of God simply as ‘the Name’.
passages.later:
The third of the Ten Commandments, on most counts, guards the same thing: “You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain” (Exodus 20:7).

The New Testament tells of two men condemned on this charge. Of Jesus the high priest said, “He has blasphemed” (Matthew 26:65). Stephen was accused of ‘words of blasphemy against Moses and against God’ (Acts 6:11) and was stoned outside the city. As he died he prayed, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:60).
passages.hard:
Why was a man put to death for cursing God in a fight?

To many modern readers the penalty seems out of all proportion, and the text does not soften it.

Several things are said in reply. In Israel God was the nation's king, and his name was bound up with his presence among the people. Cursing it struck at the covenant on which the community's life rested. The case was not decided in anger. The man was held, God's ruling was sought, and those who heard him had to stand as witnesses. The law applied to native and foreigner alike. Later Jewish tradition narrowed the offense and surrounded such cases with strict safeguards.

Christians have generally held that this penalty belonged to Israel's civil law under God's direct rule. It is not a model for the church, and it is not a model for any state. No one may use this passage to justify harming a person for what they say or believe about God.

The New Testament adds a painful turn. Jesus and Stephen were both condemned for blasphemy they had not committed. Neither answered with a curse.

The chapter still leaves a reader with a question worth facing: how seriously do I take the name of God?
passages.asks: Stephen, stoned on a charge of blasphemy, prayed for the people who were killing him. Ask how you answer when what you hold most holy is mocked. And ask how you yourself use the name of God: in prayer, in anger, or without a thought.

passages.happening:
“And if a man takes the life of anyone else, he must surely be put to death” (verse 17). Whoever kills an animal must replace it (verse 18).

“If anyone injures his neighbor, whatever he has done must be done to him: fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (verses 19-20).

“You are to have the same standard of law for the foreign resident and the native; for I am the LORD your God” (verse 22).

Then the sentence on the blasphemer is carried out (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The case of one man opens out into a statement of justice for all.

Many scholars note that these verses are shaped like a mirror. The command to punish the man and the carrying out of it stand at the two ends. Inside them stand the law on blasphemy and the rule of one law for all. Inside those, the killing of a person and of an animal. And at the very center stands ‘eye for eye’. The shape puts equal justice at the heart of the passage.

‘Eye for eye’ sounds harsh, but it was a limit. In a world of blood feuds, a family might answer one injury with a much greater one. This rule says the penalty must fit the harm and go no further. It was given to judges, not to people taking revenge for themselves.

It also applied to everyone alike. The law of Hammurabi, king of Babylon, required an eye for an eye when one nobleman blinded another, but only a payment of silver when the victim was a commoner or a slave. Leviticus has one standard, and names the foreigner first.

Jewish tradition, in the Mishnah and the Talmud, read the rule as requiring payment equal to the injury, not literal maiming, and many scholars think it worked that way in practice.

The passage also draws a firm line between a human life and an animal's. An animal can be paid for. A human life cannot be given a price.
passages.later:
‘Eye for eye’ appears three times in the law: in Exodus 21:24, here, and in Deuteronomy 19:21. In Deuteronomy it is set in a court, where “The judges shall investigate thoroughly” (Deuteronomy 19:18).

Jesus quotes it in the Sermon on the Mount: “You have heard that it was said, ‘Eye for eye and tooth for tooth.’ But I tell you not to resist an evil person” (Matthew 5:38-39). He does not abolish it as a limit for courts. He refuses to let it rule personal wrongs, and calls his followers to give up revenge.
passages.asks: The law demanded one standard for the native and the foreigner, the powerful and the weak. Ask whether you judge an offense differently depending on who did it and who suffered it. And ask where you are keeping count of wrongs done to you, and what Jesus asks of you there.
